result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.count_multiple()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Count multiple edges grouped by node pair. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L23638-L23711){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.count_multiple() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Returns a dictionary showing how many edges exist between each pair of nodes that has multiple edges. Only includes pairs with 2 or more edges. For undirected graphs, returns unordered pairs (smaller node ID first). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[tuple[int, int], int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary mapping (source_id, target_id) to edge count. Only includes pairs with count >= 2. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Aggregates the same information `which_multiple()` reports as a per-pair tally: for every endpoint pair with at least two edges, the entry $(u, v) \mapsto k$ records the exact multiplicity. Undirected graphs canonicalize each pair so the smaller node ID comes first, which lets client code index directly without worrying about orientation. Self-loops are included only when a node carries two or more of them, matching the multiplicity threshold used for ordinary pairs. Useful for planning edge consolidations, weighted rollups, or multigraph-to-weighted-graph conversions. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Rather than listing every duplicated edge, this groups them by node pair and reports how many edges connect each pair: ::: {#69787b85 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True) g.add_node(label="A") g.add_node(label="B") g.add_node(label="C") g.add_edge(source="A", target="B") g.add_edge(source="A", target="B") # Duplicate g.add_edge(source="A", target="B") # Another duplicate g.add_edge(source="B", target="C") g.add_edge(source="B", target="C") # Duplicate counts = g.count_multiple() # Convert to labels for a readable summary { (g.get_label_from_id(src), g.get_label_from_id(tgt)): count for (src, tgt), count in counts.items() } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {('A', 'B'): 3, ('B', 'C'): 2} ``` ::: ::: This is useful for planning which edges to consolidate, such as merging repeated shipping routes between the same two cities into a single weighted edge: ::: {#d0f19e70 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} transport = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="CityA") .add_node(label="CityB") .add_node(label="CityC") .add_edge(source="CityA", target="CityB", route="highway") .add_edge(source="CityA", target="CityB", route="railway") .add_edge(source="CityA", target="CityB", route="airline") .add_edge(source="CityB", target="CityC", route="highway") ) # Returns {('CityA', 'CityB'): 3} -- 3 routes to consolidate { (transport.get_label_from_id(id1), transport.get_label_from_id(id2)): count for (id1, id2), count in transport.count_multiple().items() } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {('CityA', 'CityB'): 3} ``` ::: :::
